books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, B. The American System and Sectionalism

stimulus.text:
| Tariff | Average duty on imports |
|---|---|---|
| Tariff of 1816 | about 25 percent |
| Tariff of 1824 | about 33 percent |
| Tariff of 1828 | about 43 percent |

The Tariff of 1828, the highest of the three, was called the Tariff of Abominations by its Southern critics.
stimulus.source_note: Rates: Tariff of 1816 about 25 percent (5 Steps 2024, Chapter 13); 1824 about 33 percent and 1828 about 43 percent (Carl Schurz, Speeches, Correspondence and Political Papers, vol. 5). Original table.

source: original; stimulus is a table of average tariff rates from 5 Steps 2024 Ch. 13 and Schurz's history of the tariffs
stem: Southerners called the Tariff of 1828 the Tariff of Abominations mainly because

options.text: it taxed the goods they imported while protecting Northern factories
it banned the import of all British goods outright
options.misconception: The tariff taxed imports; it banned nothing. British goods kept arriving, at higher prices.

options.text: it taxed Southern cotton exports directly
options.misconception: The tariff taxed goods entering the United States, not cotton leaving it.

options.text: it was passed without a vote in Congress
options.misconception: The tariff passed both houses of Congress; Southerners hated the result, not the procedure.

rationales.A: The South imported nearly everything it used and exported cotton. A 43 percent duty raised what planters paid while shielding Northern mills from British competition, so they named it an abomination.
rationales.B: A tariff is a tax, not a ban. British cloth and iron still came in; they simply cost Southern buyers far more.
rationales.C: The law taxed imports, not exports. Cotton left the country untaxed; the tax fell on what came back in.
rationales.D: Congress voted on the tariff, in both houses, and passed it. The Southern complaint was about what the law did, not about how it passed.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the tariff taxed. Imports, at an average of about 43 percent.
2. Ask who imported. Southern planters bought British goods and sold cotton abroad.
3. Ask who gained. Northern factories gained shelter from British competition.
4. Put it together. The South paid the tax and the North kept the benefit, so the South gave it a hateful name.
Background: the South exported raw cotton to Britain and imported manufactured goods, so a high import duty fell hardest on Southern buyers.
Remember: a nickname is an argument, so ask who coined it and what they were paying.
